title: Enter the Blank Person! — Coding Multi-Level Categorical Predictors

markdown.headingText: Enter the Blank Person! — Coding Multi-Level Categorical Predictors
markdown.markdown:
```{r}
#| echo: false
load("data/chapter3_env.RData")  # Inherit all objects from Chapter 3
```

Back when I was in elementary school, a wildly popular game swept through my peers. Its Chinese title carried an oddly charming cadence, *Children Fighting Together 2* (《小朋友齐打交2》), known internationally as *Little Fighter 2* (<https://www.lf2.net/>). I recently searched online and was delighted to find that an official-looking website still lingers on the web. I warmly recommend curious readers try it out (though do remember to come back and finish this book).

I bring up this arcade classic for two reasons: first, it was ridiculously fun; second, among its colorful roster of martial artists, there was a peculiar character whom I always called the "Blank Person" (Template). Unlike the other warriors, the Blank Person possessed no flashy magical abilities or special combo moves—only bare-knuckle punches and kicks. Amidst the vibrant cast, this minimalist, monochrome figure felt delightfully stark and out of place.

![](images/clipboard-2108693482.bmp)

Cruel as it sounds, in research design, such a Blank Person is the born-to-be, consummate control group. Think about it: we already have Helicopter People and Bag People, and we wish to evaluate their magical talent. What we urgently need is a cohort of people who possess zero gender self-identity, yet are functional human beings with all standard baseline capabilities. That way, we can isolate and evaluate the unique impact of each identity on magical talent.

Without further ado, let us add a cohort of Blank People into our ongoing dataset:

```{r}
## Generate data for 50 Blank People
set.seed(234)
df.blank <- data.frame(ID = c(101:150), iden = c(rep("Blank Person", 50)))
df.blank$magic_score <- rnorm(n = 50, mean = 95, sd = 10)

## Combine Blank People with our existing Helicopter and Bag People data
df4.1 <- df4 <- rbind(df1, df.blank)

## Verify the combined data
tail(df4)
summary(df4)
```

Let's inspect their descriptive distributions:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-responsive: true
#| out-width: "100%"

library(ggplot2)

gg <- ggplot2::ggplot(df4.1, aes(x = iden, y = magic_score, fill = iden)) +
  geom_violin(trim = FALSE, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.2, color = "black",
               position = position_dodge(0.9),
               outlier.shape = NA,
               show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.3, color = "black", show.legend = FALSE) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean, geom = "point",
    shape = 17, size = 5, color = "red",
    position = position_dodge(0.9),
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#69b3a2", "#ff9f40", "purple")) +
  guides(color = "none") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#69b3a2", "#ff9f40", "purple")) +
  labs(title = "Magic Talent Scores across Three Tribes", x = "Identity", y = "Magic Score") + 
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 3/1,
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))

plotly::ggplotly(gg)
```

Now our data is assembled, and it is time for analysis. What is our research hypothesis? Following our logic from earlier chapters, a natural hypothesis is that differences in magical talent exist among Helicopter People, Bag People, and Blank People:

$$\mu_{\text{Helicopter}} \ne \mu_{\text{Bag}} \ne \mu_{\text{Blank}}$$

The corresponding null hypothesis states that all three groups share identical magical talent:

$$H_0: \mu_{\text{Helicopter}} = \mu_{\text{Bag}} = \mu_{\text{Blank}}$$

## One-Way ANOVA with Three Levels in Action {#sec-onewayanova}

Any seasoned student will recognize this immediately as a classic one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA). While we used ANOVA in Chapter 3 to compare two groups, real-world textbooks typically showcase factors with three or more levels—precisely because ANOVA shines where the $t$-test cannot tread, evaluating omnibus differences across three or more groups simultaneously.

Let's run the ANOVA:

```{r}
## Disregard my variable naming habits; naming is governed purely by mood
my.aov4.1 <- aov(magic_score ~ iden, df4.1)
## We prefer reporting via car::Anova; reasons will be discussed later
car::Anova(my.aov4.1)
```

The omnibus test is highly significant: $F(2, 147) = 35.415, p = 2.794 \times 10^{-13}$.

However, the primary mission of this book is not merely to march you through standard ANOVA steps. In the previous chapter, we established that ANOVA and linear regression are mathematical siblings under the General Linear Model. Can we test this three-level hypothesis within a linear regression framework?

## Coding: The Magic of Transforming Categories into Continuous Predictors

To analyze differences among three groups via linear regression, our predictor is an unordered categorical variable with three levels. The primary hurdle is: how do we feed a multi-level categorical variable into a linear regression model? We touched upon this in Chapter 3 (@tip-coding1 and @tip-coding2), but back then our factor had only two levels. Now, with the intrusion of the Blank Person, our factor has three levels. What should we do?

In Chapter 2 and 3, we assigned numeric values to our two groups: Helicopter = 0, Bag = 1. A naive, instinctive impulse is simply to extend that sequence: let Blank Person = 2. Will this work? Let's test it:

```{r}
df4.1$iden_n <- c(rep(0, 50), rep(1, 50), rep(2, 50))
my.lm4.1 <- lm(magic_score ~ iden_n, df4.1)
summary(my.lm4.1)
```

Evidently, it does not. In Chapter 3, we proved that model fit in regression should match the ANOVA omnibus test. Yet here, the regression model reports $F(1, 148) = 43.41, p = 7.296 \times 10^{-10}$—completely at odds with our ANOVA result from @sec-onewayanova ($F = 35.415$). Where did things go wrong?

As emphasized earlier, a two-level categorical variable can be treated as a special "interval" variable because two points define exactly one distance. But with three groups, there are three pairwise distances: Helicopter-to-Bag, Bag-to-Blank, and Helicopter-to-Blank. Are these three distances equal? Absolutely not! Assigning $\{0, 1, 2\}$ artificially forces the distance between Helicopter and Blank to be exactly twice the distance between Helicopter and Bag. This unwarranted geometric constraint distorts the model.

In @tip-coding2, we noted that regardless of how a binary variable is coded, OLS regression always predicts the respective group means. What about this model?

```{r}
table(predict(my.lm4.1))
```

Compare these predictions with our empirical sample means:

```{r}
group_means <- aggregate(magic_score ~ iden, data = df4.1, FUN = mean)
group_means
```

They are not even remotely close! Treating three categorical levels as sequential integers prevents the regression model from recovering the actual group means.

We clearly require a principled coding scheme—one that grants multi-level factors the mathematical flexibility to enter linear regression as proper numeric predictors.

### 1. Dummy Coding

To make regression work properly, model predictions must correspond to empirical group means. Let's revisit our two-level model from Chapter 3:

```{r}
summary(lm1)
```

Our regression equation was $\hat{y} = 81.240 + 14.055x$. At $x = 0$, $\hat{y} = b_0 = 81.240$ (the Helicopter mean). At $x = 1$, $\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 = 95.295$ (the Bag mean).

What is missing now? The mean of the Blank People ($94.37$). How can we incorporate it? Sequential integers failed because categories are not equispaced. But categorical variables *are* effectively equispaced when restricted to two levels. So what if we introduce an additional indicator variable?

Suppose we keep $D_1$ (Helicopter = 0, Bag = 1, capturing the difference between Bag and Helicopter via $b_1$), and create a second variable $D_2$ (Helicopter = 0, Blank = 1, capturing the difference between Blank and Helicopter via $b_2$):

| Identity | $D_1$ (Bag vs. Heli) | $D_2$ (Blank vs. Heli) |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| Helicopter | 0 | 0 |
| Bag | 1 | — |
| Blank | — | 1 |

If we ran separate bivariate regressions for $D_1$ and $D_2$, that would merely replicate two isolated $t$-tests. We want a single omnibus model containing both predictors simultaneously:

$$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 D_1 + b_2 D_2$$

How should we code the Blank People on $D_1$, and Bag People on $D_2$?
For Helicopter People ($D_1 = 0, D_2 = 0$):
$$\hat{y}_{\text{Heli}} = b_0$$ {#eq-dc0}

For Bag People ($D_1 = 1, D_2 = x$):
$$\hat{y}_{\text{Bag}} = b_0 + b_1 + b_2 x$$
To isolate $b_1$, we simply set $x = 0$:
$$\hat{y}_{\text{Bag}} = b_0 + b_1$$ {#eq-dc1}

Likewise for Blank People on $D_1$, setting its code to 0 yields:
$$\hat{y}_{\text{Blank}} = b_0 + b_2$$ {#eq-dc2}

Behold! Our coding matrix is complete:

| Identity | $D_1$ (Bag vs. Heli) | $D_2$ (Blank vs. Heli) |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| Helicopter | 0 | 0 |
| Bag | 1 | 0 |
| Blank | 0 | 1 |

Let's test this in R:

```{r}
## Construct D1 and D2 according to the coding matrix
df4.1$D1 <- ifelse(df4.1$iden == "Plastic Bag", 1, 0)
df4.1$D2 <- ifelse(df4.1$iden == "Blank Person", 1, 0)

## Fit the regression model
my.lm4.2 <- lm(magic_score ~ D1 + D2, df4.1)
summary(my.lm4.2)
```

Compare this with our ANOVA output:

```{r}
car::Anova(my.aov4.1)
```

What a coincidence! The overall model $F$-test matches the ANOVA omnibus test down to the last decimal: $F(2, 147) = 35.415, p = 2.794 \times 10^{-13}$!

Now examine the regression coefficients against our empirical group means:

```{r}
group_means
```

The intercept $b_0 = 81.240$ is the mean of Helicopter People. From @eq-dc0, @eq-dc1, and @eq-dc2:

$$\begin{align}
b_0 &= \hat{y}_{\text{Heli}} = 81.240 \\
b_1 &= \hat{y}_{\text{Bag}} - \hat{y}_{\text{Heli}} = 95.294 - 81.240 = 14.055 \\
b_2 &= \hat{y}_{\text{Blank}} - \hat{y}_{\text{Heli}} = 94.370 - 81.240 = 13.131
\end{align}$$

Testing $b_1 = 0$ evaluates whether Bag People differ from Helicopter People; testing $b_2 = 0$ evaluates whether Blank People differ from Helicopter People.

Notice that although $b_1 = 14.055$ matches the mean difference from Chapter 2, its significance test ($t = 7.523, p = 4.91 \times 10^{-12}$) differs slightly from Chapter 2's isolated $t$-test:

```{r}
t.test(magic_score ~ iden, df1.1, var.equal = TRUE)
```

Why? Because the regression model calculates standard error by pooling residuals across *all three groups* (including Blank People). This is the hallmark of a **planned contrast**.

::: {#tip-planned-posthoc .callout-note icon="false"}
## Extension: Are Planned Contrasts Follow-ups to ANOVA? What about Post-Hoc Tests?

In traditional statistics pedagogy, instructors often teach one-way ANOVA first, followed by pairwise comparisons. Consequently, many students assume ANOVA is the indispensable starting point of all inquiry, and only after finding a significant omnibus $F$ do we proceed to inspect individual group differences.

Does this mean planned comparisons are merely an elaboration of ANOVA?

Not necessarily. Consider Fisher's Least Significant Difference (LSD). LSD is essentially Student's $t$-test using the pooled within-group mean square ($MS_{\text{Within}}$) from the omnibus ANOVA to estimate standard error: $SE = \sqrt{MS_{\text{Within}}\left(\frac{1}{n_i} + \frac{1}{n_j}\right)}$.

Let's compute Fisher's LSD:

```{r}
DescTools::PostHocTest(my.aov4.1, method = "lsd")
```

Compare the $p$-values with our dummy coding regression output above: they are identical! Once again, we touched the elephant without even trying.

However, Fisher's LSD is widely discouraged in contemporary practice because it does not control the family-wise Type I error rate. With three pairwise tests at $\alpha = 0.05$, the probability of committing at least one false positive across the family of tests is:

```{r}
1 - 0.95^3
```

Nearly 14.3%—almost triple our nominal 5% threshold! With more groups, error inflation escalates exponentially. This is why post-hoc tests require family-wise error rate control.[^chap4-2]

[^chap4-2]: If you ask why researchers routinely print massive correlation matrices with dozens of tests without Bonferroni correction... that is a great question. All I can say is: behold the chasm between theoretical ideals and empirical reality.

The most transparent and conservative post-hoc correction is the **Bonferroni correction**, which divides the nominal alpha evenly across all $c$ tests: $\alpha_{\text{per-test}} = \alpha / c$.

```{r}
DescTools::PostHocTest(my.aov4.1, method = "bonferroni")
```

Returning to planned comparisons: must a planned contrast be performed only after a significant ANOVA?

Absolutely not! If your theoretical hypothesis specifically predicts a difference between Bag and Helicopter People, that hypothesis stands on its own conceptual footing. Planned contrasts are guided by *a priori* theory, not by fishing through empirical ANOVA results. You can conduct planned contrasts before ANOVA, after ANOVA, or without ever running an omnibus ANOVA at all.
:::

In dummy coding, for a factor with $k$ levels, we construct $k - 1$ indicator variables.[^chap4-3] We select one level as the baseline (coded as 0 across all dummy variables), and assign a 1 to each remaining level on its designated indicator:

[^chap4-3]: Why $k - 1$? Because $k$ group means represent $k$ pieces of information. The intercept consumes one piece of information ($b_0$), leaving $k - 1$ degrees of freedom for slopes.

| Factor Level | $D_1$ | $D_2$ | $\dots$ | $D_{k-1}$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Reference Baseline | 0 | 0 | $\dots$ | 0 |
| Level 2 | 1 | 0 | $\dots$ | 0 |
| Level 3 | 0 | 1 | $\dots$ | 0 |
| $\dots$ | $\dots$ | $\dots$ | $\dots$ | $\dots$ |
| Level $k$ | 0 | 0 | $\dots$ | 1 |

At the start of this chapter, we introduced Blank People as a natural control group. Let's place Blank People at the intercept baseline ($D_1 = D_2 = 0$):

| Identity | $D_{1n}$ (Bag vs. Blank) | $D_{2n}$ (Heli vs. Blank) |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| Helicopter | 0 | 1 |
| Bag | 1 | 0 |
| Blank (Baseline) | 0 | 0 |

```{r}
df4.1$D1n <- ifelse(df4.1$iden == "Plastic Bag", 1, 0)
df4.1$D2n <- ifelse(df4.1$iden == "Attack Helicopter", 1, 0)

my.lm4.3 <- lm(magic_score ~ D1n + D2n, df4.1)
summary(my.lm4.3)
```

The omnibus model fit remains identical ($F = 35.41$). Intercept $b_0 = 94.37$ is the mean of Blank People. The slope $D_{1n} = 0.924, p = 0.622$ shows that Bag People do not significantly differ from Blank People, whereas Helicopter People score significantly lower ($D_{2n} = -13.131, p = 7.26 \times 10^{-11}$). Identifying as a Helicopter suppresses magical talent relative to baseline, whereas identifying as a Plastic Bag offers no special magical boost!

::: {#tip-dcal .callout-tip icon="false"}
## Food for Thought: What If We Don't Code Blank as 0 on Both?

What happens if we deviate from standard dummy coding? For example:

| Identity | $R_1$ | $R_2$ |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| Helicopter | 0 | 0 |
| Bag | 1 | 0 |
| Blank | 1 | 1 |

```{r}
df4.1$R1 <- c(rep(0, 50), rep(1, 50), rep(1, 50))
df4.1$R2 <- c(rep(0, 50), rep(0, 50), rep(1, 50))
my.lm4.4 <- lm(magic_score ~ R1 + R2, df4.1)
summary(my.lm4.4)
```
What specific pairwise comparisons do $R_1$ and $R_2$ test here? Work through the algebra to find out!
:::

### 2. Effects Coding (Deviation Coding)

At the start of this chapter, we praised Blank People as an ideal control group. But in reality, control groups are rarely pristine. Suppose that one day, the Blank People achieve political consciousness and declare that their blank identity is not an "absence of identity," but an affirmative identity in its own right. Those treacherous Blank People have sabotaged our control group!

In real-world research—especially with demographic variables like ethnicity or nationality—a pure control group rarely exists. How can we test how each group performs relative to the *average* across all groups?

In effects coding, we set the baseline to the **unweighted grand mean** of all groups:

$$\begin{align}
b_0 &= (\hat{y}_{\text{Heli}} + \hat{y}_{\text{Bag}} + \hat{y}_{\text{Blank}}) / 3 \\
b_1 &= \hat{y}_{\text{Bag}} - b_0 \\
b_2 &= \hat{y}_{\text{Heli}} - b_0
\end{align}$$ {#eq-effect}

Solving for the group predictions in terms of coefficients:[^chap4-7]

[^chap4-7]: I strongly encourage readers to grab pen and paper to verify this derivation.

$$\begin{align}
\hat{y}_{\text{Bag}} &= b_0 + b_1 \\
\hat{y}_{\text{Heli}} &= b_0 + b_2 \\
\hat{y}_{\text{Blank}} &= b_0 - b_1 - b_2
\end{align}$$

To achieve this in regression, our coding matrix must assign $-1$ to the reference group:

| Identity | $E_1$ | $E_2$ |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| Helicopter | 0 | 1 |
| Bag | 1 | 0 |
| Blank (Reference) | -1 | -1 |

Let's test effects coding in R:

```{r}
df4.1$E1 <- ifelse(df4.1$iden == "Plastic Bag", 1, 
                   ifelse(df4.1$iden == "Blank Person", -1, 0))
df4.1$E2 <- ifelse(df4.1$iden == "Attack Helicopter", 1, 
                   ifelse(df4.1$iden == "Blank Person", -1, 0))

my.lm4.5 <- lm(magic_score ~ E1 + E2, df4.1)
summary(my.lm4.5)
```

Look at the coefficients:
- Intercept $b_0 = 90.3014$: the unweighted grand mean across all three tribes ($81.24 + 95.29 + 94.37) / 3$.
- $E_1 = 4.9930$: the deviation of Bag People from the grand mean ($95.294 - 90.301 = +4.993$).
- $E_2 = -9.0618$: the deviation of Helicopter People from the grand mean ($81.240 - 90.301 = -9.062$).

Both coefficients are statistically significant, proving that both Bag and Helicopter People diverge significantly from the general average.

### 3. Contrast Coding

Beyond dummy and effects coding, we have an exceptionally versatile tool: **Contrast Coding**.

While dummy coding tests pairwise comparisons between single levels, planned contrasts frequently compare *combinations* of groups (e.g., comparing the combined average of Helicopter and Bag People against Blank People).

Suppose our research hypothesis posits that the two traditional tribes differ from the newly emergent Blank People:

$$\frac{\mu_{\text{Heli}} + \mu_{\text{Bag}}}{2} - \mu_{\text{Blank}} \ne 0$$

Multiplying by 2 to clear fractions:

$$1 \cdot \mu_{\text{Heli}} + 1 \cdot \mu_{\text{Bag}} - 2 \cdot \mu_{\text{Blank}} \ne 0$$

In general, any linear contrast hypothesis takes the form:

$$L = w_1 \mu_1 + w_2 \mu_2 + \dots + w_k \mu_k \ne 0$$

Here, $w_1 = 1, w_2 = 1, w_3 = -2$. To complete the system, we add a second contrast comparing the two traditional tribes to each other:

$$1 \cdot \mu_{\text{Heli}} - 1 \cdot \mu_{\text{Bag}} + 0 \cdot \mu_{\text{Blank}} \ne 0$$

| Identity | $C_1$ | $C_2$ |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| Helicopter | 1 | 1 |
| Bag | 1 | -1 |
| Blank | -2 | 0 |

::: callout-tip
## Food for Thought: Planned vs. Post-Hoc Comparisons in a 5-Level Design
Suppose an experiment has 1 control group ($A$) and 4 treatment groups ($B, C, D, E$). If the researcher only cares about $A-B, A-C, A-D, A-E$, can they simply run four pairwise comparisons? Should they first test an omnibus contrast like $(4, -1, -1, -1, -1)$? Ponder how family-wise error control intersects with theoretical intentionality.
:::

Let's test our contrast matrix in R:

```{r}
df4.1$C1 <- ifelse(df4.1$iden == "Plastic Bag", 1, 
                   ifelse(df4.1$iden == "Blank Person", -2, 1))
df4.1$C2 <- ifelse(df4.1$iden == "Attack Helicopter", 1, 
                   ifelse(df4.1$iden == "Blank Person", 0, -1))

my.lm4.6 <- lm(magic_score ~ C1 + C2, df4.1)
summary(my.lm4.6)
```

Examining the regression coefficients:

```{r}
compr_value1 <- group_means[group_means$iden == "Plastic Bag", "magic_score"] +
                group_means[group_means$iden == "Attack Helicopter", "magic_score"] -
                2 * group_means[group_means$iden == "Blank Person", "magic_score"]
compr_value1
compr_value1 / 6
```

The coefficient $b_1 = -2.034$ equals the contrast value divided by 6 ($\sum w_i^2 = 1^2 + 1^2 + (-2)^2 = 6$). Dividing by a constant scalar does not alter the $t$-statistic or $p$-value.

Now, consider what happens if we chose a different second contrast: comparing Bag People directly to Blank People:

| Identity | $C_1$ | $C_{2n}$ |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| Helicopter | 1 | 0 |
| Bag | 1 | 1 |
| Blank | -2 | -1 |

```{r}
df4.1$C2n <- ifelse(df4.1$iden == "Attack Helicopter", 0, 
                    ifelse(df4.1$iden == "Blank Person", -1, 1))

my.lm4.7 <- lm(magic_score ~ C1 + C2n, df4.1)
summary(my.lm4.7)
```

Look at the coefficient for $C_1$: it jumped from $-2.034$ to $-9.062$, even though we did not alter the coding for $C_1$ at all! Why did $C_1$'s value morph?

#### Orthogonality of Contrast Variables

This introduces the golden rule of contrast coding: contrast vectors must be **orthogonal**.

Two contrast vectors $C_1$ and $C_2$ are orthogonal if and only if:
1. The weights within each contrast sum to zero: $\sum w_{1j} = 0$ and $\sum w_{2j} = 0$.
2. The sum of their pairwise cross-products equals zero:

$$\sum_{j=1}^{k} w_{1j} w_{2j} = 0$$

Check our first contrast coding:
- Helicopter: $1 \times 1 = 1$
- Bag: $1 \times (-1) = -1$
- Blank: $(-2) \times 0 = 0$
- Sum: $1 + (-1) + 0 = 0$. **Orthogonal!**

Now check our flawed second contrast coding:
- Helicopter: $1 \times 0 = 0$
- Bag: $1 \times 1 = 1$
- Blank: $(-2) \times (-1) = 2$
- Sum: $0 + 1 + 2 = 3 \ne 0$. **Non-orthogonal!**

When contrasts are non-orthogonal, collinearity entangles their regression slopes: the estimate for $b_1$ becomes contaminated by $b_2$. Orthogonality guarantees that each contrast partitions an independent, additive slice of sum of squares without mutual interference.[^chap4-12]

[^chap4-12]: A moral takeaway: in statistics as in life, keep relationships clean and straightforward, lest entanglements corrupt your results.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Food for Thought: Can Random Coding Return in Multi-Level Designs?

In Chapter 3 (@tip-coding1), we showed that any two distinct arbitrary numbers produce identical omnibus model fit. Does this hold for three levels if we assign completely random values across two coding columns?

```{r}
df4.1$R1 <- c(rep(1, 50), rep(20, 50), rep(300, 50))
df4.1$R2 <- c(rep(233, 50), rep(666, 50), rep(4396, 50))
my.lm2.8 <- lm(magic_score ~ R1 + R2, df4.1)
summary(my.lm2.8)
```

Indeed, the omnibus $F$-statistic and $R^2$ remain identical. What mathematical conditions must a coding matrix satisfy to preserve omnibus ANOVA equivalence?
:::

### Unbalanced Sample Sizes and Coding

In experimental psychology, balanced sample sizes ($n_1 = n_2 = \dots = n_k$) are convenient, but observational data is frequently unbalanced (e.g., female-to-male ratios in psychology majors).

Let's artificially trim our dataset to create an unbalanced sample of 120 individuals (40 Helicopter, 50 Bag, 30 Blank):

```{r}
df4.2 <- df4.1[df4.1$ID < 131 & df4.1$ID > 10, ]
group_means2 <- aggregate(magic_score ~ iden, data = df4.2, 
                          FUN = function(x) c(mean = mean(x), n = length(x)))
group_means2
```

Does sample imbalance bias regression estimates of group means?

```{r}
my.lm4.9 <- lm(magic_score ~ D1 + D2, df4.2)
summary(my.lm4.9)
```

The estimated group means remain perfectly unbiased because OLS minimization operates on each group independently.

However, a fundamental distinction emerges regarding the grand mean:

1. **Unweighted Grand Mean**: treating each group as an equal conceptual unit:

$$\bar{Y}_{\text{Unweighted}} = \frac{\bar{Y}_{\text{Bag}} + \bar{Y}_{\text{Heli}} + \bar{Y}_{\text{Blank}}}{3}$$ {#eq-unweighted}

2. **Weighted Grand Mean**: weighting each group mean by its sample size:

$$\bar{Y}_{\text{Weighted}} = \frac{n_1 \bar{Y}_1 + n_2 \bar{Y}_2 + n_3 \bar{Y}_3}{n_1 + n_2 + n_3}$$ {#eq-weighted}

```{r}
## Unweighted mean
mean(group_means2[, 2][, 1])

## Weighted mean
(group_means2[group_means2$iden == "Attack Helicopter", 2][, 1] * 40 +
 group_means2[group_means2$iden == "Plastic Bag", 2][, 1] * 50 +
 group_means2[group_means2$iden == "Blank Person", 2][, 1] * 30) / 120
```

In standard contrast and effects coding, regression intercepts estimate the **unweighted** grand mean. In most psychological research, unweighted means are preferred because sample size discrepancies are typically sampling artifacts rather than meaningful population proportions.

#### Designing Weighted Contrasts

When sample sizes genuinely reflect population proportions (such as stratified sampling across demographic cohorts), we can design custom **weighted contrasts**:

$$\begin{align}
b_0 &= (40\hat{y}_{\text{Heli}} + 50\hat{y}_{\text{Bag}} + 30\hat{y}_{\text{Blank}}) / 120 \\
b_1 &= (40\hat{y}_{\text{Heli}} + 50\hat{y}_{\text{Bag}}) / 90 - \hat{y}_{\text{Blank}} \\
b_2 &= \hat{y}_{\text{Heli}} - \hat{y}_{\text{Bag}}
\end{align}$$

Solving this linear system yields the weighted contrast weights:

| Identity | $CW_1$ | $CW_2$ |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| Helicopter | 1/4 | 5/9 |
| Bag | 1/4 | -4/9 |
| Blank | -3/4 | 0 |

```{r}
df4.2$CW1 <- ifelse(df4.2$iden == "Attack Helicopter", 1/4, 
                    ifelse(df4.2$iden == "Blank Person", -3/4, 1/4))
df4.2$CW2 <- ifelse(df4.2$iden == "Attack Helicopter", 5/9, 
                    ifelse(df4.2$iden == "Blank Person", 0, -4/9))

my.lm4.11 <- lm(magic_score ~ CW1 + CW2, df4.2)
summary(my.lm4.11)
```

Notice the intercept: $b_0 = 90.2292$—matching our weighted grand mean exactly!

By mastering dummy coding, effects coding, orthogonal contrast coding, and weighted systems, you can translate any substantive theoretical hypothesis directly into the General Linear Model.
